weakness: The program detected the plate once, before picking up the spoon, and released the spoon at that position; the plate had been slid 7 cm while the spoon was being picked, so every spoon landed 7 cm off the plate centre.
how_found: Questioned A1: the goal location was perceived once at the start of a multi-second manipulation; on a real robot a person or another process can move the target while the arm is busy.
why_missed: The first version treated the goal pose as fixed scene knowledge read once, because nothing moved in the nominal scenes.
fix: Detect the plate after the pick, tracking it over short windows until it is stationary; check it again right before releasing and carry the spoon over its new position if it moved more than 1.5 cm.
general_rule: Re-perceive the goal location right before acting on it and after every long step, waiting until it is stationary, instead of reusing an estimate taken before the manipulation began.

weakness: The program took every grasp from the object's annotated grasp frames. With the spoon lying upside down those frames pointed into the counter, every candidate's pre-grasp pose was below the counter top, and the program gave up without trying any other grasp.
how_found: Questioned A4: the grasp library assumes the object rests in its nominal orientation, and on a real counter utensils and tools are often flipped or turned on their side.
why_missed: In every nominal scene the object rested the right way up, so the library grasp always produced a reachable candidate and I never checked what it depended on.
fix: When the library grasp finds no candidate, derive a top-down grasp from the current bounding box: vertical approach onto the object's frame point, fingers closing across its longest horizontal axis, fingertips just above its underside.
general_rule: Do not depend on one grasp source tied to an object's nominal pose; when it yields nothing, derive a grasp from the object's currently observed geometry, approaching vertically and closing across its narrow horizontal dimension just above its underside.

weakness: The program trusted a single top-down pinch of a heavier, slippery spoon: the grip held for the first 1-2 cm of the lift, then the spoon slid down out of the fingers. The program repeated near-identical grasps, and its own fallback grasp descended so close to the counter that the planner refused the last centimetres.
how_found: Questioned A5: a top-down pinch of a flat object holds it by friction alone, and real utensils are wet, greasy or heavier than the nominal one.
why_missed: The nominal spoon weighs 50 g, so any pinch held it, and I never checked a grasp before carrying the object.
fix: Lift 3 cm and check the hold before the full lift; on a slip, release, detect again and re-grasp differently (at the box centre as a centre-of-mass guess, at another fingertip height, shifted along the object); let the short final descent of the fallback grasp touch the counter so that it is not refused. A wrist roll that put a finger under the object did not help and was removed.
general_rule: Check every grasp with a short test lift before carrying, and when the object slips, change the grasp (nearer the centre of mass, another contact height or position) instead of repeating the one that just failed.

weakness: With the spoon partly under a low overhang, every grasp the program tried was under or right next to the overhang: the library grasp and the grasp at the object's frame point were blocked, and their partial descents pushed the spoon further in. The exposed end (7.5 cm) is shorter than the hand needs (about 6 cm along the object plus the planner's safety margin), so even a grasp chosen there by a clearance check, vertical or tilted 20-35 degrees from the open side, was refused on its approach.
how_found: Questioned A4: the program assumed there is room for the hand above its grasp point; on real counters utensils lie partly under shelves, boards and other items.
why_missed: In the nominal scenes nothing is above the spoon, so I never checked the space the hand needs before reaching.
fix: Not recovered in 3 repairs (best 0.0): a clearance check over the hand's footprint along the object, checking that space before any reach, a tilted approach from the open side, and stopping when the object has been knocked off the counter. Moving the object into the open first (a push) would also need the hand next to the overhang. Variation reverted; the pipeline is back at round 3.
general_rule: Before reaching, check that the whole hand plus the planner's safety margin fits around the grasp point, because a reach that is refused halfway still pushes the object deeper into clutter; if no point on the object has that room, the object must be moved into the open before it can be grasped.

weakness: The same weakness as v8 with more of the spoon exposed (about 10 cm of the bowl end): the program's grasps are at or near the spoon's middle, under the overhang, and a refused reach still pushes the spoon. Choosing a grasp point on the exposed end by checking the space above it recovered 3 of 10 seeds; most approaches to that end were still refused or used up the episode budget.
how_found: Repeated v8's question (room for the hand above the grasp point) with an exposure long enough for the hand, to separate 'no room anywhere' from 'room, but not where the program grasps'.
why_missed: The program never asked where on the object there is room for the hand; its re-grasps only move 3 cm along the object.
fix: Not recovered in 2 repairs (best 0.3): grasp points along the object filtered by the hand's footprint against the obstacle boxes, checked before any reach (0.3); the footprint widened by the planner's margin (0.2, more episodes out of budget). The approach of the whole arm, not only the hand, has to clear the overhang. Variation reverted; the pipeline is back at round 3.
general_rule: Before reaching, check that the whole hand plus the planner's safety margin fits around the grasp point, because a reach that is refused halfway still pushes the object deeper into clutter; if no point on the object has that room, the object must be moved into the open before it can be grasped.
